--- Page 1 ---
RadonBench: A Benchmark of Classical and Learning-Guided
Search Techniques for Problems in Combinatorial Geometry
Xiaoan Xu∗, Jesus A. De Loera†, Ethan X. Fang‡, Junwei Lu§, Luze Xu¶
Abstract
Classical optimization and learning-guided search offer complementary approaches to open
problems in discrete mathematics, but their outputs are difficult to compare when search spaces,
validity checks, and stopping rules differ. We present RadonBench, a benchmark for constructing
maximum-cardinality Radon-free lattice configurations: finite subsets of Zd admitting no integral
Radon partition. It remains open whether Radon-free configurations with 11 points in Z3 or 21
points in Z4 are possible. If they exist, they would improve the corresponding lower bounds on
the integer Radon numbers. We compare exhaustive extension, greedy local search, PatternBoost,
AlphaZero, and AlphaEvolve. All outputs use one success predicate: a convex target-sized
configuration succeeds exactly when its number of integral Radon points is zero. PatternBoost
and AlphaZero construct verified Radon-free configurations of sizes 10 and 20, one point short
of the respective targets; AlphaZero’s best convex target terminals have two integral Radon
points in both dimensions. Exhaustive extension over fixed seeds and declared finite search boxes
likewise reaches a minimum of two integral Radon points. Greedy local search and AlphaEvolve
each produce target-sized near misses with one integral Radon point. No audited run reaches zero.
These results establish reproducible near-miss baselines over explicitly scoped search domains.
1
Introduction
Mathematical discovery is rapidly changing with tools from AI. Classical enumeration and local
optimization, neural construction, search with learned policies, and evaluator-guided program
evolution have all proved useful for combinatorial discovery [Wagner, 2021, Fawzi et al., 2022,
Charton et al., 2024, Novikov et al., 2025].
Despite this progress, many basic combinatorial
quantities, including numerous Ramsey numbers, remain beyond the reach of both conventional
computation and current AI-assisted methods [Radziszowski, 1994, McKay and Radziszowski, 1995,
Exoo, 1989]. Here we investigate another equally difficult problem and use it to benchmark modern
search techniques.
Radon’s theorem is a fundamental result in convex and discrete geometry: any d + 2 points in
Rd admit a bipartition whose convex hulls intersect [Bárány, 2021, Barvinok, 2002, Gruber, 2007].
Motivated by applications in integer programming and combinatorics, researchers have studied
integer versions of Radon’s theorem [Onn, 1991, Eckhoff, 1993, De Loera et al., 2017, 2019]. Here
the points have integer coordinates, and the intersection of the two convex hulls must contain a
lattice point. This gives an integral Radon partition. A finite set in Zd with no such partition is

§Department of Biostatistics, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.

Figure 1: The search problem. (a) Onn’s five-point configuration in Z2 is Radon-free [Onn, 1991].
(b) An 11-point near-miss in Z3 found by the declared local-search experiment. The displayed split
has the single shared lattice point p = (3, 2, 0), hence nrp = 1; success requires nrp = 0.
Radon-free, and the integer Radon number r(Zd) is the smallest cardinality for which every lattice
point configuration has an integral Radon partition. The exact value in the plane is r(Z2) = 6, but it
remains unknown in higher dimensions [Onn, 1991, Bezdek and Blokhuis, 2003]. We study whether
there is a Radon-free configuration with 11 points in Z3 or one with 21 points in Z4.
The search for Radon-free configurations offers a compact comparison setting: candidate verifica-
tion is practical, yet the configuration space is already too large for naive enumeration at the open
targets. Prior work established structural bounds and recognition complexity for integral Radon
partitions [Onn, 1991, Bezdek and Blokhuis, 2003], but those authors did not systematically study
constructive search near the open lattice frontiers.
We introduce RadonBench, a benchmark of five method families: exhaustive extension, greedy
local search, a task-adapted PatternBoost solver, AlphaZero-Radon (our AlphaZero-style solver),
and AlphaEvolve-style program evolution. These methods instantiate two complementary search
paradigms. Cardinality constructors grow configurations point by point while maintaining Radon-
freeness at every proper prefix; PatternBoost and AlphaZero-Radon belong primarily to this group.
Fixed-target optimizers instead evaluate complete N-point configurations and minimize their number
of integral Radon points; this group comprises exhaustive extension, greedy local search, and
AlphaEvolve-style program evolution. AlphaZero-Radon is construction-oriented but also scores
convex N-point terminals, so it contributes to the fixed-target comparison whenever it reaches the
horizon. The methods do not search one common finite domain and their computational units are
not matched. We therefore compare verified outputs rather than claim a ranking of search efficiency.
In particular, we separate two questions:
RQ1 Does any declared protocol produce a verifier-accepted configuration at an open target?
RQ2 If a run is unsuccessful, what does it nevertheless certify: the largest verified Radon-free cardinality
kmax, or the minimum target-sized Radon-point count rmin(N)?
This separation prevents a legal (N −1)-point prefix from being treated as a scored N-point candidate.
Explicit 10-point and 20-point witnesses provide finite-box positive controls immediately below the
two frontiers; smaller cardinalities need not be benchmarked separately because Radon-freeness is
2


--- Page 3 ---
hereditary.
Our contributions are twofold. First, we define a common success predicate, graded score, and
reporting contract for search methods with different proposal spaces. Second, we give an auditable
outcome comparison across five classical and learning-guided method families in Z3 and Z4, while
making each method’s reachable configurations and stopping conditions explicit. Verifier derivations,
hyperparameter tables, search-space diagnostics, and additional experiments are provided in the
appendices.
No audited run reported here resolves either open frontier. All negative observations are limited
to the candidates or finite domains searched by the declared protocols; they are not non-existence
results for Z3 or Z4.
2
Problem and Evaluation
Let X ⊂Zd be a finite set of distinct points. An integral Radon partition is a split X = A ⊔B
into nonempty parts satisfying conv(A) ∩conv(B) ∩Zd̸ = ∅. We call every lattice point in such an
intersection an integral Radon point and write
nrp(X) = #{p ∈Zd : p is an integral Radon point of X}.
Thus X is Radon-free exactly when nrp(X) = 0. Every such configuration is in convex position:
if x ∈conv(X \ {x}), then {x} ⊔(X \ {x}) already has the shared lattice point x. Known global
bounds establish the existence of Radon-free sets through sizes 10 in Z3 and 20 in Z4, while N = 11
and N = 21 are the respective open targets [Onn, 1991, Bezdek and Blokhuis, 2003]. Separate
explicit witnesses certify those two feasible cardinalities immediately below the open targets.
Shared verification.
Every reported output is judged by the same two-stage evaluator: it first
checks convex position and then enumerates lattice points in conv(X) and tests whether each
supports an integral Radon partition. A candidate succeeds only if it has the target cardinality, is in
convex position, and has nrp = 0. The full evaluator and audit procedure appear in Appendix C.1.
For each lattice point p ∈(conv(X) ∩Zd) \ X, the evaluator tests whether there are weights
λi ≥0 and binary assignments bi ∈{0, 1} satisfying
P
i biλixi = p,
P
i(1 −bi)λixi = p,
P
i biλi = 1,
P
i λi = 2.
Here bi = 1 assigns xi to one side of the partition and bi = 0 assigns it to the other. The first two
equalities express the same point p as a convex combination of the two sides. The third equality
normalizes the first combination; together with P
i λi = 2, it also makes the coefficients of the second
combination sum to one. Thus both sides are nonempty, and feasibility holds exactly when p is an
integral Radon point for some partition. PyNormaliz enumerates the candidate lattice points and
Gurobi performs these split tests [Bruns and Ichim, 2010, Gurobi Optimization, LLC, 2026]. Each
feasible p is counted once, irrespective of how many partitions witness it, and their number is nrp.
The input points are omitted because the preceding convex-position check guarantees that none lies
in the convex hull of the others.
Output semantics.
A single leaderboard would conflate variable-length construction with fixed-
target repair. For audited outputs O of a declared run, we therefore report
kmax = max{|X| : X ∈O, X convex, nrp(X) = 0},
rmin(N) = min{nrp(X) : X ∈O, |X| = N, X convex}.

The second quantity is undefined if no convex target candidate is emitted. Method-native counts
and layer profiles describe outputs but are not pooled into cross-method success rates. Search
boxes, proposal domains, stopping rules, and budgets are stated per method; shared verification
makes certificates and scores comparable, not search coverage or efficiency. Appendix B.1 gives the
finite-box witnesses, and Appendix C records the per-method configurations.
3
Methods
All five methods use the target cardinality and verifier from Section 2. For a method with an origin-
anchored finite coordinate domain of side lengths L = (L1, . . . , Ld), we write Λ(L) = Qd
j=1{0, . . . , Lj−
1}. No single box is shared across methods: each protocol has the method-specific coordinate domain
listed in Table 1, and the program-evolution method has no finite coordinate bound. Box membership
is part of success only when the method itself enforces it.
Exhaustive extension and greedy local search are classical methods; PatternBoost, AlphaZero-
Radon, and AlphaEvolve-style program evolution are learning-guided. By search objective, Pattern-
Boost and AlphaZero-Radon are primarily cardinality constructors, while exhaustive extension, local
search, and program evolution optimize complete N-point configurations. AlphaZero-Radon also
scores the terminal configuration when it reaches N. The methods differ in their one-step proposals
and reachable states, summarized in Table 2; these restrictions scope every negative result. In
Table 2, “Starts from” denotes an externally supplied configuration; deterministic protocol anchors
are specified in the method descriptions.

3.1
Shared interface
Every method calls the shared convex-position and Radon-point evaluator described in Section 2.
A proposal may emit a complete configuration or build/edit one sequentially. Reported outputs
use the same success predicate, and every retained coordinate array is replayed with the reference
evaluator. The exact implementation and the exhaustive driver’s equivalent convex-position test are
documented in Sections C.1 and C.2.
3.2
Exhaustive add-one-point
For each of 50 fixed Radon-free (N −1)-point seeds S, this baseline tests every unoccupied position
q in a declared finite box Bd and retains convex extensions. Its per-seed objective is
mBd(S) =
min
q∈Bd\S:
S∪{q} in convex position
nrp(S ∪{q}) .
(1)
“Exhaustive” therefore means exhaustive over the final point after fixing S and Bd, not over all seeds
or all N-point configurations. Exact boxes, coverage counts, and pseudocode are given in Table 1
and section C.2.
3.3
Greedy local search
This deterministic-after-initialization repair baseline starts from a convex N-point extension of a
stored Radon-free (N −1)-point configuration. A sweep visits points in stored order and evaluates
all full-coordinate radius-one moves
xi + δ,
δ ∈{−1, 0, 1}d \ {0},
that remain distinct, convex, and inside the method’s box. It accepts the admissible move with
the lowest strictly smaller nrp, using a fixed direction order for ties, and stops at nrp = 0, after a
non-improving sweep, or after 100 sweeps. Because it changes one point at a time and rejects plateaus
5


--- Page 6 ---
and temporary increases, it cannot make coordinated moves or cross score barriers. Initialization
and ordering details are in Section C.3.
3.4
PatternBoost generation
Our PatternBoost track is an iterative construction–training loop adapted from Charton et al. [2024].
Configurations in Λ(L) are encoded as mixed-radix point-token sequences. Generation 0 greedily
grows empty states by accepting an addition only when the new prefix is convex and has nrp = 0.
The largest terminal states are retained, symmetry-augmented, and used to train a decoder-only
Transformer [Vaswani et al., 2017]; sampled sequences seed the next generation and are completed by
the same greedy legality test. The model is therefore trained as an ordering prior, while the verifier
enforces every constraint. Here nrp is a gate rather than a graded objective: an illegal addition is
rejected, and construction stops when no tested point extends the prefix. Tokenization, selection,
and training details are in Section C.4.
3.5
AlphaZero-style construction: AlphaZero-Radon
AlphaZero-Radon is a task-specific adaptation of the AlphaZero algorithmic template [Silver et al.,
2018], not a reuse of its chess, shogi, or Go model. It retains policy–value-guided PUCT and an
iterative search–training loop, but replaces the original game representation and residual convolutional
network. Our single-agent construction task uses unordered point-set states, a permutation-invariant
set-attention policy–value network [Lee et al., 2019], lattice-cell actions, and verifier-defined outcomes.
Each trajectory starts at the fixed origin and adds the remaining points in Λ(L). The network scores
lattice locations, and Monte Carlo tree search plans with the shaped edge reward
r(s′) =














0
if s′ is not in convex position,
CR
N(1 + nrp(s′))
if s′ is convex and nrp(s′) > 0,
CS
N
if |s′| = N, s′ is convex, and nrp(s′) = 0,
Cstep
N
if |s′| < N, s′ is convex, and nrp(s′) = 0.
(2)
with Cstep = 1, CR = 2, and CS = 25. A non-convex or Radon-positive state terminates the
simulated branch; convex Radon-positive states receive the displayed graded terminal reward at
every cardinality. We report fixed-target quality only for convex terminals at the horizon.
To control branching, each expanded node retains the K = 64 unoccupied actions with the largest
network probabilities. A child found terminal during search is marked and skipped by subsequent
tree selections. Each decision uses 500 simulations, after which the trajectory generator samples
from the root visit distribution at temperature one. Training, architecture, and the exact Plan-D
search procedure are specified in Section C.6.
3.6
AlphaEvolve-style program evolution
AlphaEvolve [Novikov et al., 2025] treats executable programs, rather than point sets, as the
population under search. We instantiate this with OpenEvolve [Sharma, 2025]: an LLM proposes
exact search-and-replace edits to a Python block, a fixed evaluator executes the edited constructor,
and an island-based MAP-Elites archive [Mouret and Clune, 2015] retains programs by both fitness
and behavioural features. Thus PatternBoost models a distribution over point sequences, whereas
the AlphaEvolve-style method evolves the algorithm that constructs or repairs point sets.
6


--- Page 7 ---
The immutable wrapper gives each program sixteen fixed Radon-free (N −1)-point references
and the verifier. One evaluation permits at most 1,000 find_rps calls and returns at most 32 integer
N × d candidates. Only four constructor functions may evolve; the wrapper, resource accounting,
geometry code, and external evaluator remain fixed. The initial program implements the interface
but emits no candidate, so it contributes no hand-written search heuristic.
After the allowance closes, the evaluator validates shapes, finiteness, integrality and distinctness,
then recomputes convexity and nrp for every returned candidate. Program fitness is the maximum
score of one candidate; statistics from different candidates are never mixed. A convex target with
k > 0 Radon points scores 0.50 + 0.49/(1 + k); a convex Radon-free target scores 1. The full fitness,
evolution loop, and audit fields are given in Section C.5.
4
Results
The five methods share one headline question: did the declared run produce a verifier-accepted
configuration at the open target? Table 3 therefore reports target recovery first. When a run does
not recover the target, it keeps two secondary outcomes in separate columns: kmax, the largest fully
Radon-free configuration emitted at any cardinality, and rmin(N), the smallest verifier score among
emitted convex target-sized configurations. These quantities describe different output types and are
not combined into a cross-method ranking.

RQ1: Did a protocol recover an open-target counterexample?
No completed PatternBoost
run, exhaustive add-one-point experiment, AlphaZero-Radon run, 1,000-start greedy-local-search
run, or AlphaEvolve-style program-evolution run produces a verified open-target counterexample.
RQ2: What certified output did an unsuccessful run produce?
PatternBoost reaches
kmax = 10 in Z3 and 20 in Z4. Across its complete 2,000-iteration runs, AlphaZero-Radon reaches
kmax = 10 in 3D and 20 in 4D; among its convex target terminals, the minimum score is 2 in both
dimensions. Exhaustive add-one-point search also attains minimum score 2 in both dimensions after
covering every extension position in each of its 50 fixed-seed boxes. Greedy local search attains score
1 in both dimensions (on 27 of 1,000 3D terminals and 25 of 1,000 4D terminals), but never reaches
zero. The AlphaEvolve-style method likewise attains rmin = 1 in both dimensions: its best programs

The experiments are not compute- or verifier-query-matched. Method-native run lengths and
budgets are reported for reproducibility, but Table 3 compares verified outputs rather than search
efficiency. Appendix A records the completed runs and retained outputs.
5
Related Work
Onn formalized integral Radon partitions in the lattice setting, proved r(Z2) = 6, established general
bounds, and studied recognition complexity [Onn, 1991]. Bezdek and Blokhuis proved the upper
bound r(Z3) ≤17 [Bezdek and Blokhuis, 2003]; integral Radon partitions are also integer 2-Tverberg
partitions [De Loera et al., 2017]. These works motivate the open frontiers but do not provide a
multi-method empirical study of constructive search.
Relevant ingredients in machine-assisted mathematical discovery include neural construction [Wag-
ner, 2021], policy–value-guided tree search from AlphaZero [Silver et al., 2018], its task-specific
adaptation to algorithm discovery in AlphaTensor [Fawzi et al., 2022], Transformer-guided search
[Charton et al., 2024], and LLM program evolution [Romera-Paredes et al., 2024, Novikov et al.,
2025]. A recent comparative precedent studies classical, PatternBoost, and reinforcement-learning
methods for the no-three-in-line problem [Ramanathan et al., 2025]. RadonBench instead uses a
lattice-convexity verifier and explicitly separates constructive from fixed-cardinality outputs. Com-

plete computational resolutions of combinatorial existence problems require exhaustive search and
checkable certificates [Heule et al., 2016, Heule, 2018, Brakensiek et al., 2022]; our bounded searches
do not provide such a non-existence certificate.
6
Discussion
Neither PatternBoost, exhaustive extension, nor AlphaZero-Radon reaches an open target; greedy
local search likewise finds no target across 1,000 starts per dimension but reaches score-one near
misses in both. Two explanations remain inseparable: the declared searches may cover too little of
their method-specific domains, or a Radon-free configuration may not exist at that cardinality. These
observations support only search-space diagnoses. A constructor’s legal-prefix frontier reflects its
proposal distribution and cutoff, not a global obstruction. After 20 mutations, the AlphaEvolve-style
runs in both dimensions reach score-one near misses.
Reading the results through each search space.
Exhaustive extension provides a finite-domain
completeness statement only after fixing a legal (N −1)-point seed and a finite box for the last point.
The completed experiment visits every position in each declared box, but its negative result concerns
only those 50 fixed seeds per dimension, not configurations that require changing a seed or adding a
point outside the box.
Greedy local search has the opposite search-space design. It can modify every coordinate of every
point of an N-point configuration over successive sweeps, but each proposal moves only one point by
Chebyshev radius one, remains inside the fixed box, and must immediately lower the integer-valued
score. All 2,000 reported runs stall at positive score, including 27 of 1,000 in 3D and 25 of 1,000
in 4D at score one. A missing path may therefore require coordinated changes, a neutral or uphill
intermediate state, or leaving the declared box.
9


--- Page 10 ---
PatternBoost and AlphaZero-Radon both build point sets sequentially. PatternBoost assigns no
graded score to a failing prefix, whereas AlphaZero-Radon gives a larger terminal reward to a convex
Radon-positive state with fewer integral Radon points. PatternBoost fits an ordering distribution
from previously retained configurations and then uses the verifier to accept or skip sampled points.
AlphaZero-Radon uses its policy to retain a top-K action set at each expanded node and spends
MCTS simulations only within that restricted support. A frontier at N −1 therefore means that the
learned proposal mechanism did not produce a verified continuation under the declared run; it is not
evidence that no continuation exists elsewhere in the box.
AlphaEvolve-style program evolution has the broadest coordinate interface because an evolved
program may emit arbitrary finite integer coordinates. Its practical search space is nevertheless the
set of programs reached by its declared mutation lineage and the bounded batch of candidates each
program returns. Its 3D and 4D lineages both attain one-Radon-point target configurations, but
neither returns a Radon-free target. These distinctions are why we keep target recovery, valid-prefix
cardinality, and target-sized score in separate table columns rather than treating the five methods as
an efficiency leaderboard.
What defines a reproducible search-space claim.
A finite-box exhaustive search must specify
its fixed seeds and coordinate box; a repair method must specify its initialization, move radius,
number of points changed together, and acceptance rule. A learned constructor additionally needs
its action vocabulary, candidate truncation, and terminal handling, while program evolution needs
its evaluator batch and number of mutations. Omitting any of these choices changes the reachable
candidates. We expose them so future runs can vary one restriction at a time without changing the
success predicate. The same accounting explains why a grid position, a repair trajectory, an MCTS
game, and a program-returned candidate are not interchangeable trials.
A complete negative result would require more than exhaustive evaluation inside one coordinate
box. One would need a proved finite representative family, or an invariant coordinate bound, for lower-
cardinality Radon-free configurations and a proved finite extension region for every representative.
Affine unimodular transformations preserve Radon-freeness but need not preserve a box, so bounded-
box exhaustion alone does not cover all equivalence classes. The appendices state the exact scope of
every filled result.
Implications for search design.
The framework suggests three protocol-level choices for future
runs. First, repair methods should test coordinated moves or permit neutral and uphill transitions
instead of enlarging the coordinate radius alone. Second, initialization and box constraints deserve
the same care as the stopping rule because both restrict reachable basins. Third, evaluation should
retain the objective each algorithm actually optimizes. Constructors should report the largest
verified legal prefix, whereas fixed-target methods should report the best verified target score; neither
replaces the common binary target-recovery outcome.
Limitations.
The methods use different proposal domains, move sets, and run lengths; hardware
and verifier calls are not matched. PatternBoost has one 20-generation run per dimension, and
AlphaZero-Radon has one complete 2,000-iteration cold-start run per dimension. AlphaEvolve-style
program evolution has one 20-mutation lineage per dimension rather than repeated independent trials.
The greedy-local-search results are limited to 1,000 fixed starts per dimension, strict single-point
descent, and dimension-specific fixed boxes. The exhaustive experiment fixes only 50 catalog seeds
per dimension and cannot exclude extensions of other seeds or points outside its declared boxes.
Consequently, Table 3 compares verified outputs, not sample or computational efficiency. Although
10


--- Page 11 ---
the two constructive methods share the 6 × 6 × 6 × 6 box in 4D, their search distributions and
budgets are not matched.
7
Conclusion
RadonBench organizes five classical and learning-guided searches around a common target-recovery
criterion while preserving their different output semantics. PatternBoost reaches the known cali-
bration cardinalities 10 and 20; across its complete 2,000-iteration runs, AlphaZero-Radon reaches
the same cardinalities and target score 2 in both dimensions, while exhaustive add-one-point search
obtains target score 2 but no target recovery after completely visiting the declared box for each of
50 fixed seeds in both dimensions. Full-coordinate greedy local search reaches score 1 but no target
across 1,000 starts per dimension. AlphaEvolve-style program evolution also reaches score 1 in both
dimensions after 20 mutations, without recovering either target. These results do not resolve the
integer Radon numbers, but the success-first reporting scheme provides a reproducible framework
for adding future searches without conflating solution quality with compute efficiency.

the project “AI Foundation Models for Reasoning in Polyhedral Geometry.”

A
Detailed Experimental Outcomes
All declared runs use the stopping rules and sample counts specified in the method appendix. The
headline outcomes appear in Table 3; this section records only method-native evidence that is not
shown there.
A.1
Constructive methods
PatternBoost.
Both 20-generation loops completed. In the 20 × 20 × 5 box, the largest verified
Radon-free cardinality is 10; generation 20 retains 47 ten-point and three nine-point states. In the
6 × 6 × 6 × 6 box, the largest cardinality is 20, reached in generations 12, 13, 15, and 18; generation
20 retains eight nineteen-point, 19 eighteen-point, and 23 seventeen-point states. Neither run reaches
its open target.
AlphaZero-Radon.
Each 2,000-iteration run generates 200,000 trajectories. In 3D, 157,485
trajectories reach the 11-point horizon and 8,651 of those terminals are convex; their minimum score
is rmin(11) = 2. In 4D, 120,973 trajectories reach the 21-point horizon and 2,302 are convex; their
minimum score is rmin(21) = 2. The largest verified Radon-free prefixes have 10 and 20 points,
respectively, and neither run reaches its open target.
A.2
Fixed-target methods
Exhaustive extension.
For each dimension, the experiment fixes 50 Radon-free seeds and tests
every unoccupied lattice position in the declared box. The 3D run tests 159,500 additions and scores
85,913 convex targets; the 4D run tests 499,000 additions and scores 173,355 convex targets. The
minimum score is two in both dimensions. This is exhaustive only for the fixed seed–box pairs.
Greedy local search.
Both dimensions use fixed 1,000-start evaluation sets. In 3D, 990 starts
improve and 27 terminate at score one; the median score falls from 10 to 4. In 4D, 991 starts improve
and 25 terminate at score one; the median falls from 15 to 4. Neither run reaches zero. The reported
4D aggregate is fixed to indices 0–999.
AlphaEvolve-style program evolution.
Each dimension has one 20-mutation lineage. Every
completed mutation returns 32 convex target-sized configurations under a shared allowance of 1,000
internal find_rps calls, for 640 externally scored candidates per dimension. Neither lineage reaches
zero. The first score-one program appears at mutation 7 in 3D and mutation 11 in 4D.

Additional Experiment Configurations
Software.
Python 3.11.15, NumPy 2.4.6, PyNormaliz 2.23, Gurobi 13.0.2. The structural analyses
use no GPU; all analysis runs on CPU on a shared machine, so wall-clock figures are indicative

Figure 4 gives eight verified 10-point configurations in Λ(20, 20, 5). PB-A–PB-D are retained outputs

to expose different layerwise structures, not to estimate how frequently either method produces a
profile. The reference verifier independently confirms convex position and nrp = 0 for every displayed
configuration.
16


--- Page 17 ---
B.3
Result aggregation and audit
For constructive protocols, we replay retained serialized terminal states and take the largest cardinality
passing convexity and nrp = 0; this produces kmax in Table 3. For fixed-target protocols, we discard
repeated-row or non-convex arrays and take the minimum nrp among the remaining N-point
candidates; this produces rmin(N) in Table 3. Ties may be resolved by lexicographic order of the
sorted integer rows when an exact representative is needed. Each reported result records its source
run, iteration or generation, verifier output, and artifact path. AlphaZero-Radon aggregation includes
all 2,000 completed iterations in each dimension.
C
Implementation details
This appendix provides pseudocode for the reference verifier and every evaluated search method.
The complete algorithmic specifications appear in Algorithms 1 to 7.
C.1
Reference verifier
The benchmark verifier consists of the functions is_conv_position_all() and find_rps(). For
X = {x1, . . . , xn} ⊂Zd, the first routine performs one leave-one-out linear-program feasibility test
per input point. For each i, it asks whether coefficients αj ≥0 exist such that
X
j̸=i
αj = 1,
X
j̸=i
αjxj = xi.
(3)
Feasibility means xi ∈conv(X \ {xi}) and the candidate is rejected; is_conv_position_all()
returns True exactly when every leave-one-out model is infeasible.
The function find_rps() first passes the homogenized polytope to PyNormaliz [Bruns and
Ichim, 2010] and reads Deg1Elements, which enumerates the lattice points in conv(X). Input vertices
are removed. For every remaining lattice point p, the verifier asks whether there are λi ≥0 and
binary bi ∈{0, 1} such that
X
i
biλixi = p,
X
i
(1 −bi)λixi = p,
X
i
biλi = 1,
X
i
λi = 2.
(4)
The variable bi assigns xi to the first part when bi = 1 and to the second part when bi = 0; the
corresponding products select the weights used by each convex combination. The first coefficient sum
is constrained to one, and the second also sums to one because P
i(1−bi)λi = P
i λi−P
i biλi = 2−1.
Thus a feasible solution places p in the convex hulls of two nonempty disjoint parts. Conversely, any
integral Radon partition and an integral Radon point give a feasible assignment. The implementation
solves this model with Gurobi [Gurobi Optimization, LLC, 2026], sets NonConvex=2 for the binary–
continuous products, and tests each candidate p. It returns each feasible lattice point once, irrespective
of the number of partitions that witness it; hence the benchmark score is nrp(X) = |find_rps(X)|.
A candidate is a verified Radon-free configuration exactly when is_conv_position_all() returns
True and find_rps() is empty.
17


--- Page 18 ---
Algorithm 1 Reference convexity and integral-Radon-point evaluator.
Require: finite set of distinct lattice points X = {x1, . . . , xn} ⊂Zd
Ensure: convex-position flag c and set R of integral Radon points
1: for i = 1, . . . , n do
2:
if xi ∈conv(X \ {xi}) according to Equation (3) then
3:
return (False, ∅)
4:
end if
5: end for
6: P ←(conv(X) ∩Zd) \ X using PyNormaliz
7: R ←∅
8: for p ∈P do
9:
if the feasibility system in Equation (4) accepts p then
10:
R ←R ∪{p}
11:
end if
12: end for
13: return (True, R)
Following the canonical implementation, Infeasible rejects a candidate Radon point and every
other returned status counts it. All complete Radon-count evaluations use this same rule.
Cross-track accounting.
The five tracks are not compute-matched. Method-native stopping
rules are part of each protocol, but raw verifier-call totals are not used as a common budget or
efficiency metric. Reported local-search aggregates are computed from retained JSON/NPZ artifacts
for both the 3D and 4D instances; retained outputs likewise support both dimensional instances of
the other tracks. A stochastic run is successful only if a serialized candidate passes the common
verifier.
The available implementations use the software versions listed below and in Section C.3. Their
evaluator implementations share the formulation and status rule above. Retained configurations and
aggregate logs support the reported audits.
PatternBoost and AlphaZero-Radon environment.
PatternBoost and AlphaZero-Radon
use Python 3.11.15, PyTorch 2.12.0 with CUDA 13.0, NumPy 2.4.6, SciPy 1.17.1 (including Qhull),
PyNormaliz 2.23, and Gurobi 13.0.2. Neural-network training and generation use one NVIDIA
A100-SXM4 GPU with 80 GB memory; CPU processes execute the geometric oracle. We do not
request PyTorch’s bitwise-deterministic GPU kernels.
Local
and
exhaustive
environment.
These CPU-only searches use Python 3.12.11,
NumPy 1.26.4, SciPy 1.16.2, PyNormaliz 2.19, and Gurobi 12.0.3; the local-search environment
also contains PyTorch 2.8.0 and trimesh 4.8.3. They run on an Intel Xeon Gold 5320 node (two
26-core sockets, SMT2, 503 GiB RAM). Local tasks request 32 CPUs and 64 GB with at most three
concurrent tasks; exhaustive tasks request 8 CPUs and 24 GB and run one at a time. Neither
requests a GPU.
Program-evolution environment.
OpenEvolve uses Python 3.12.11, OpenEvolve 0.2.27,
NumPy 1.26.4, SciPy 1.16.2, PyNormaliz 2.19, and Gurobi 12.0.3 on the same CPU node. Each job
requests four CPUs, 64 GB RAM, and no GPU. The method-specific subsections give the remaining
seeds, stopping rules, provenance, and run settings.

--- Page 19 ---
Algorithm 2 Exhaustive add-one-point search within a fixed box
Require: verified Radon-free seed S ⊂Zd with |S| = N −1; bounds (ℓj, uj)d
j=1
Ensure: minimum score m, minimizers Q, score histogram H, coverage counts
1: B ←Qd
j=1{ℓj, . . . , uj}; m ←+∞; Q ←∅; H ←∅; cconvex ←0
2: for q ∈B in Cartesian-product order do
3:
if q ∈S then
4:
continue
5:
end if
6:
X ←S ∪{q}
7:
if X is not in convex position then
8:
continue
9:
end if
10:
cconvex ←cconvex + 1
11:
r ←nrp(X); H[r] ←H[r] + 1
12:
if r < m then
13:
m ←r; Q ←{q}
14:
else if r = m then
15:
Q ←Q ∪{q}
16:
end if
17: end for
18: return (m, Q, H, |B| −|S|, cconvex)
C.2
Exhaustive add-one-point experiment configuration
Dimension-general procedure.
For a fixed seed S ⊂Zd and integer box B = Qd
j=1{ℓj, . . . , uj},
the driver visits every q ∈B in deterministic Cartesian-product order. It skips q ∈S, rejects
extensions outside convex position, and evaluates nrp(S ∪{q}) for every remaining extension. It
does not stop when a zero or a new minimum is found. Therefore every unoccupied position in B is
either rejected by the convex-position predicate or assigned a Radon-point count. This is the sense
in which the search is exhaustive. The seed is never modified, and no claim is made about other
seeds or positions outside B.
Frozen seeds and sampling.
Before evaluation, the experiment fixes 50verified Radon-free seeds
per dimension using NumPy seed 20260819. The 3D seeds lie in {−10, . . . , 9}2 × {0, . . . , 7}; the
4D seeds lie in {0, . . . , 19}2 × {0, . . . , 4}2. Seed selection is independent of extension scores, and no
sampling occurs during a task.
Boxes and coverage.
The 3D box is B3 = {−10, . . . , 9} × {−10, . . . , 9} × {0, . . . , 7}, with 3,200
positions. Each 10-point seed is contained in B3, leaving 3,190 attempted additions per seed and
159,500 overall. The 4D box is B4 = {0, . . . , 19} × {0, . . . , 19} × {0, . . . , 4}2, with 10,000 positions.
Each 20-point seed is contained in B4, leaving 9,980 attempted additions per seed and 499,000
overall.
Convex-position and Radon tests.
Before enumeration, the driver checks that the seed is row-
distinct, in convex position, and has nrp(S) = 0. For each extension X, it constructs the homogenized
polytope with PyNormaliz and reads ExtremeRays. The extension passes exactly when the returned
rays equal {(x, 1) : x ∈X}, so every input point is a vertex. This exact rational extreme-ray test
19


--- Page 20 ---
is mathematically equivalent to the reference leave-one-out convex-position predicate, although
it is a different implementation. For every passing extension, find_rps_nd() uses PyNormaliz
Deg1Elements and the same Gurobi partition-feasibility test in Section C.1. Gurobi uses one thread
per model; up to eight lattice points are tested concurrently within a task.
The supplementary manifest records the fixed seed coordinates, declared boxes, and coverage
counts needed to reproduce the reported aggregate.
C.3
Greedy local-search experiment configuration
Dimension-general procedure.
For an instance (d, N, L), the descent moves all coordinates. Its
ordered neighbourhood is
Dd = {−1, 0, 1}d \ {0}.
For a box Λ(L), proposals outside the box are rejected. The evaluated 3D and 4D neighbourhoods
contain 26 and 80 offsets, respectively, before boundary and geometry filtering. The method uses
a strict-improvement rule, stored point order, lexicographic direction order, a 100-sweep cap, and
early stopping at score zero or after a full non-improving sweep.
Initial configurations.
In 3D, initialization adds one uniformly sampled point in {−10, . . . , 9}2 ×
{0, . . . , 4} to a verified 10-point seed and accepts the first distinct, convex extension within 100
draws. From the eligible pool, 1,000starts are sampled with NumPy seed 20260819 and translated
into the 20 × 20 × 5 box. In 4D, one uniformly sampled in-box point is added to each verified
20-point seed, again requiring distinctness and convex position; the reported set is the fixed first
1,000starts generated with NumPy seed 20260815. Initialization does not filter or rank candidates
by nrp. Algorithm 3 gives the subsequent deterministic descent. The point order is the stored array
order. Directions are the lexicographically ordered Cartesian product {−1, 0, 1}d with the zero vector
removed. Only strict improvement is admissible, so the first direction attaining a given best score
wins a tie and equal-score plateaus are never traversed. No anchoring translation occurs during
descent. All accepted 3D configurations remain inside {0, . . . , 19}2 × {0, . . . , 4}, and all accepted 4D
configurations remain inside {0, . . . , 19}2 × {0, . . . , 4}2.
Convexity and score implementation.
For every candidate, convex position is checked point by
point. To test point xi, a Gurobi feasibility LP asks whether nonnegative coefficients on X \{xi} sum
to one and reproduce xi; feasibility rejects the candidate. For the objective, PyNormaliz enumerates
the degree-one lattice points of the homogenized polytope and the implementation removes the input
vertices. For each remaining lattice point p, Gurobi solves the feasibility model
X
i
biλixi = p,
X
i
(1 −bi)λixi = p,
X
i
biλi = 1,
X
i
λi = 2,
with λi ≥0 continuous and bi ∈{0, 1}; the model uses NonConvex=2. The number of feasible p
is the descent score; any solver status other than Infeasible is treated as feasible. No Gurobi
feasibility, integrality, or optimality parameters are overridden. Radon points are memoized within
a configuration after its first score evaluation. The fixed selection manifests identify the 1,000
reported starts in each dimension, and the retained trajectories reproduce the aggregate outcomes in
Appendix A. The CPU implementation uses Python 3.12.11, PyNormaliz 2.19, Gurobi 12.0.3, and
SciPy 1.16.2.

C.4
PatternBoost experiment configuration
For an instance (d, N, L), PatternBoost uses variable-length add-point sequences in Λ(L).
Its
vocabulary has 1 + Qd
j=1 Lj entries: one shared Start/Stop token and one token per lattice point.
A sequence has the form [0, τL(p1), . . . , τL(pk), 0], where the points are sorted lexicographically
before supervised training; losses after the first stop token are masked. The reference incremental
legality test accepts a prefix only when it is in convex position and has no integral Radon point.
This is stricter than merely filtering complete model outputs: every training configuration and
every saturated output is legal at each accepted prefix. All dimension-independent architectural,
21


--- Page 22 ---
optimization, selection, generation, and saturation hyperparameters are shared across dimensions.
The completed three-dimensional run instantiates L = (20, 20, 5) and N = 11, giving a 2,001-
token vocabulary. The completed four-dimensional run uses L = (6, 6, 6, 6) and N = 21, giving a
1,297-token vocabulary.
Algorithm 4 PatternBoost with verifier-gated incremental saturation.
Require: box L, maximum size N, generations G, state-batch size B, keep fraction q, target
retained-set size T, reference predicate Legal(S)
1: form T/q independent empty seeds; saturate each seed with Legal
2: retain the top qB terminal states within each batch to obtain D0
3: for i = 0, . . . , G −1 do
4:
split Di by complete symmetry orbit into train/validation sets
5:
augment both splits by box-preserving reflections and axis permutations
6:
train a next-token Transformer; retain the lowest-validation-loss checkpoint
7:
sample T/q unconstrained token sequences from Start
8:
decode each sequence in order, skipping a token unless it denotes an unused lattice point
whose addition satisfies Legal
9:
for each decoded seed state S do
10:
while |S| < N and untested lattice points remain do
11:
traverse the remaining points in a fresh random order
12:
append the first p with Legal((S ∪{p})); permanently remove every tested point,
including p, from the remaining pool
13:
stop if no tested point is legal
14:
end while
15:
end for
16:
in each batch of B terminal states, retain the top qB states by cardinality
17:
Di+1 ←retained states; save their unaugmented and augmented forms
18: end for
Teacher forcing pads every sequence to context length N + 1 (12 in 3D and 22 in 4D). For an
ordered point-token sequence (τ1, . . . , τk), the input is [0, τ1, . . . , τk] and the target is [τ1, . . . , τk, 0];
target positions after the first stop are set to −1 and ignored by cross-entropy. Minibatches are
sampled uniformly with replacement.
Let mℓbe the multiplicity of side length ℓin L. The augmentation group has
|H(L)| = 2d Y
ℓ
mℓ!
box-preserving transformations: independent reflections and permutations among axes with equal
side lengths. All transforms are emitted without deduplicating coincident arrays. For L = (20, 20, 5)
this gives 16 transforms; for L = (6, 6, 6, 6) it gives 244! = 384. With 50 retained configurations, the
nominal 45/5 orbit split yields 720/80 augmented train/validation sequences in 3D and 17,280/1,920
in 4D when all orbits are distinct. Complete symmetry orbits are assigned wholly to one split before
augmentation. Validation evaluates at most ten batches of 100. Training runs for 500 updates and
evaluates every 25 updates; the minimum validation-loss checkpoint among steps 25, 50, . . . , 500 is
used both for generation and to initialize the next round. Exact split sizes and selected steps are
recorded per generation.
The Transformer uses learned token and absolute-position embeddings, untied output weights,
causal self-attention, and PyTorch’s default parameter initialization. Its dropout rate is zero. At

Generation always draws N tokens after the initial Start, without constraining the vocabulary,
in minibatches of 10. Decoding stops at the first sampled Stop; before that stop, duplicate or illegal
point tokens are removed from the remaining-point pool and skipped while later tokens are still
attempted. Saturation repeatedly draws a fresh permutation of the remaining pool, accepts the first
legal point, and permanently removes all points tested in that pass. The 250 terminal states form
one selection batch; the largest 20%, namely 50 states, survive. Stable input order breaks cardinality
ties. Generation and saturation use 16 CPU workers. A master seed of 20260809 initializes Python,
NumPy, and PyTorch randomness; per-state seeds are assigned before parallel dispatch.
C.5
AlphaEvolve-style program-evolution experiment configuration
Dimension-general task interface.
For every instance (d, N), the immutable wrapper receives
the same typed inputs: sixteen cataloged (N −1) × d arrays encoding Radon-free configurations, the
dimension-independent geometry routines, target size N, output cap, and remaining oracle allowance.
Returned candidates must have shape N × d. The mutable four-function interface, validation order,
fitness, oracle allowance, output cap, and MAP-Elites mechanism are shared across dimensions.
The dimension, target, reference catalog, feature-bin count for best_size, and number of evolution
mutations are recorded separately below. No lattice side lengths are passed to the evolved program
or enforced by the evaluator.
Dimension-specific inputs.
The 3D run samples eight references from each of two catalogs of
verified 10-point configurations; the 4D run samples sixteen references from a catalog of verified
20-point configurations. Both use selection seed 2026, run for 20mutations, and accept arbitrary
23


--- Page 24 ---
finite integer output coordinates. The completed runs take 4.88 and 47.58 hours in 3D and 4D,
respectively.
Each call to generate_candidates installs process-local wrappers around the geometry functions.
Calls to find_rps while the candidate program is active increment a counter and are limited jointly
to 1,000; after exhaustion, a further call returns a nonempty sentinel rather than permitting a false
Radon-free result. Convexity calls are uncharged. The internal allowance closes before the external
evaluator begins, so rechecking the returned batch neither consumes nor enlarges the program’s
search budget. Every program receives a newly initialized NumPy default_rng(42) and may return
at most 32 arrays.
Candidate validation and fitness.
The evaluator imports the generated module and invokes
generate_candidates(N,32); the declared three-dimensional instance instantiates this call with
N = 11. Exceptions receive score 0 and an error flag. Each returned object is converted to a
NumPy array and rejected unless it is finite, two-dimensional with d columns, integer-valued, and
row-distinct. More than 32 objects are truncated; arrays with a row count other than N receive
candidate score 0. For a target-sized array X = (x1, . . . , xN), let P = (x1, . . . , xN−1) denote its
ordered prefix. The exact candidate score is
s(X) =












0.50 + 0.49/(1 + nrp(X)),

0.40 + 0.09((N −1)/N),
X is not convex, but P is convex and nrp(P) = 0,
0,
otherwise.
(5)
The program fitness combined_score is maxX s(X) over the returned batch. The evaluator records
the best candidate and summary batch statistics; no metric combines properties from different
candidates.

Require: instance (d, N), initial program p0, fixed evaluator E, islands I, number of mutations T,
target fitness 1
1: evaluate p0 with E; insert its source, metrics, and features into the database
2: for t = 1, . . . , T do
3:
choose the active island and sample a parent from its population/archive
4:

5:
request an exact SEARCH/REPLACE diff from gpt-5.6-sol
6:

7:
execute the child with a fresh RNG seed 42 and a shared allowance of 1,000 internal find_rps
calls

E independently validates and scores at most 32 returned candidates
9:
store source, parent, prompt, response, metrics, features, and candidate artifact

update the island and global archive; migrate after every ten island generations
11:

12: end for

Outcomes.
Each AlphaEvolve-style program-evolution experiment completes 20 mutations.
Every child in both runs returns 32 convex target configurations, uses exactly 1,000 internal oracle
calls, and has evaluator error flag zero. Each lineage therefore returns 20 × 32 = 640 candidates.
Neither returns a Radon-free target. The best 3D program (first seen at mutation 7) and best 4D
program (first seen at mutation 11) each attain one Radon point and fitness 0.745.
C.6
AlphaZero-Radon experiment configuration
The reported runs use the Plan-D search and training implementation.
The 3D instance has
L = (20, 20, 5), N = 11, and 2,000 actions. The 4D instance has L = (6, 6, 6, 6), N = 21, and 1,296
actions. Both complete 2,000 iterations, comprising 200,000 generated trajectories per dimension; all
completed iterations enter the reported outcomes. The implementation calls this data-generation
phase “self-play,” but the adapted task is single-agent and has no opponent.
States, actions, and terminal outcomes.
A state is the unordered set of placed lattice points,
serialized internally by mixed-radix tokens
a(x) =
d
X
j=1
xj
j−1
Y
k=1
Lk,
so the first axis varies fastest. Every game starts from the fixed origin (0, . . . , 0) and the agent selects
the remaining N −1 points. The origin is an explicit finite-box anchor, not a without-loss-of-generality
reduction; it contributes neither a policy target nor an edge reward. At an expanded node, occupied
actions are zeroed before candidate ranking. Applying an action terminates the branch when the
new set is non-convex, has positive nrp, or reaches N. Rewards follow Equation (2) and are attached
to the edge entering the successor. The value head estimates the undiscounted future reward-to-go.
Plan-D top-K PUCT.
Let Pθ(· | s) be the full-vocabulary softmax policy. Every newly expanded
node zeros occupied actions, retains the K = 64 largest remaining probabilities, and renormalizes
them. Writing the retained support as C(s), the tree prior is
bP(a | s) = Pθ(a | s)1{a ∈C(s)}
P
b∈C(s) Pθ(b | s)
.
25


--- Page 26 ---
At the root only, self-play replaces this prior by 0.75 bP + 0.25η, where η ∼Dir(0.11). There is no
eager root probe: a transition is checked only when tree selection reaches it. Once a child is found
terminal, Plan D marks that edge and excludes it from later tree selections. Terminal means any
non-convex or Radon-positive set as well as a target success, so a scored terminal receives one backup
before it is masked. Search does not stop early upon discovering a success.

PUCT and training targets.
PUCT uses
Q(s, a) =
W(s, a)
1 + N(s, a),
U(s, a) = bP(s, a)
p
N(s)
1 + N(s, a).
The root visit count starts at zero. Each simulation accumulates normalized per-edge rewards
between the leaf and every ancestor and adds Vθ only at a nonterminal leaf. After 500 simulations,
the root visit counts are normalized over the full vocabulary and the played action is sampled from
them with T = 1.
For a minibatch of size B, define the full-vocabulary policy by
pθ(a | sb) =
exp ℓθ(sb, a)
P
c∈Λ(L) exp ℓθ(sb, c).
The loss is
L = −1

Here λV = 20, πb is the normalized MCTS visit vector, and Gb is the undiscounted reward-to-go.
Although πb is sparse because search expands top-K actions, the softmax denominator is the full
action vocabulary.
Network.
Each coordinate is normalized as uj = xj/(Lj −1) and mapped to the Fourier feature
vector
[sin(2kπuj), cos(2kπuj)]Bd−1
k=0 ,
where the Nyquist-safe Bd = 3 in both runs, followed by a learned linear projection to width
256. Four layer-normalized set-attention blocks with four heads encode the placed-point set. Each
multihead-attention block uses scaled dot-product attention, a query residual, a ReLU output
projection with a second residual, and LayerNorm after each residual. Every candidate cell uses
the same coordinate encoder to form a cross-attention query over the set latents; a 256 →256 →1
GELU MLP produces its policy logit. The value head mean-pools the set latents and applies an
independent 256 →256 →1 GELU MLP, whose scalar output is used directly. All linear layers use
PyTorch defaults, and the dropout rate is zero.
Replay and optimization.
One randomly initialized network and one Adam optimizer persist
across all iterations. At each iteration, every self-play game receives the latest evaluation-mode
weights, and every move constructs a fresh tree. Deterministic verifier outcomes may be memoized
within a trajectory; this does not alter transitions, terminal labels, rewards, or the search budget.
For each decision after the origin, self-play stores the pre-move token set, the normalized visit
policy, the final Radon count, and the reward-to-go.
The learner appends the current iteration before training. For each of ten updates, it selects a set-
length bucket with probability proportional to its buffered sample count and draws min(128, |bucket|)
examples uniformly without replacement. Thus each iteration makes at most 1,280 replay draws,
independent of the current FIFO population; samples may reappear in later updates. Adam uses
the fixed learning rate 10−4, PyTorch defaults for (β1, β2, ϵ), and coupled ℓ2 weight decay 10−4.
Both jobs run uninterrupted from a clean initialization to iteration 2,000. The global initialization
seed is 42; per-game and replay-sampling seeds are deterministic functions of the iteration and game
indices. End-to-end wall times are approximately 85.9 hours in 3D and 561.4 hours in 4D.

Figure 5: Training diagnostics for the complete 2,000-iteration AlphaZero-Radon runs. The top and
bottom rows show the 3D (N = 11) and 4D (N = 21) instances, respectively. Curves are 50-iteration

Aggregation over the complete runs.
In 3D, 157,485 of 200,000 generated trajectories place
an eleventh point. Of those terminals, 8,651 are convex and receive a complete Radon count; the
minimum is 2. In 4D, 120,973 games place a twenty-first point, 2,302 of those terminals are convex,
and the minimum Radon count is 2; a trajectory with terminal score two first appears at iteration
702. No target terminal has score zero. The remaining target-cardinality terminals are non-convex
and are not included in the “target candidates” column. The largest fully verified prefixes have
sizes 10 and 20, respectively. Figure 5 reports the corresponding optimization and trajectory-length
diagnostics over the same complete runs.
